subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Choice Overload in Stores
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Choice Overload in Stores.

hook.text: Iyengar set up a jam tasting booth. 24 jams attracted more visitors but 6 jams generated 10 times more purchases.

buildup.text: Choice overload: too many options paralyze decision-making. The effort to compare exceeds the motivation to choose.

discovery.text: Schwartz calls this the paradox of choice. More options increase regret because every choice has more attractive.

twist.text: Smart retailers cut visible options. Curated selections guide buyers to confident purchases.

climax.text: When overwhelmed by options, set criteria first: budget, features, purpose. Then eliminate. Do not compare. Eliminate.

punchline.text: The best choice is often fewer choices.

quiz.question: What happened in Iyengar's jam study with 24 options?
options: Sales were 10 times higher than with 6 options
More visitors sampled but far fewer purchased

details.summary: Choice overload occurs when too many options overwhelm consumers, leading to decision paralysis, lower satisfaction, and fewer purchases. The famous jam study showed that 24 jam varieties attracted browsers but 6 varieties drove ten times more sales.
details.whyItMatters: Retailers must balance variety with simplicity. Too many options drive customers away or reduce satisfaction with their eventual choice. Understanding choice overload helps design product lines that maximize both engagement and conversion.
takeaways: Excessive options can reduce purchase rates and satisfaction
The jam study demonstrated choice overload in a real retail setting
Categorization and curation reduce overload without limiting options

faq.question: How many options is the right number for consumers?
faq.answer: Research suggests three to five options per category is optimal for most decisions. Beyond that, comparison becomes exhausting. However, the ideal number depends on expertise, product category, and how options are organized.

faq.question: How can stores offer variety without causing overload?
faq.answer: Categorizing products, highlighting a recommended option, using progressive disclosure, and providing comparison tools all help. The key is making the decision process manageable, not eliminating options entirely.
